svg.metadata:
# FigDown — figures as text. Spec: https://github.com/FigDown/figdown
figdown 0.4 sequence title "All twelve interaction operators, on one session"
# ── What this figure is ───────────────────────────────────────────── # `fragment … type=` takes one of TWELVE values, and the set is taken # whole from UML 2.5.1's InteractionOperatorKind literals rather than # picked from: `alt` `opt` `loop` `par` `strict` `seq` `critical` `neg` # `assert` `ignore` `consider` `break`. Six of them are what Mermaid # documents (loop, alt, opt, par, critical, break); the other six are # what taking the enumeration whole buys, and a value nothing in the # corpus writes is a value nobody has read. # # So this figure is the DEMONSTRATOR for the enum: one small session — # a client opening a session with a service that keeps an audit log — # with every one of the twelve stated on the part of that session where # it is actually true. The subject is chosen to be ordinary on purpose; # what is being shown is the OPERATOR, and an operator whose example # needs a paragraph of protocol to justify it teaches the protocol # instead. # # THE ORDER BELOW IS THE SESSION'S, NOT THE ENUM'S. A figure whose rows # are alphabetical is a table, and this one has a time axis that means # something. The enum order is in the paragraph above; the ladder order # is: loop, alt, assert, neg, critical, par, strict, seq, opt, break, # ignore, consider. # # EACH OPERATOR IS USED FOR WHAT IT MEANS, and the guard or the label # says which meaning: # loop the operand repeats; the guard carries the bound # alt at most ONE operand runs, chosen by the guards # opt one operand, run or not run # par the operands interleave in any order # strict the operands are TOTALLY ordered, across all lifelines # seq weak sequencing — ordered per lifeline, not between # critical the operand's occurrences may not be interleaved # neg the operand's traces are INVALID — they must not happen # assert the operand's traces are the ONLY valid continuation # ignore the named messages may occur and are insignificant # consider only the named messages are significant; others are not # break the operand runs INSTEAD OF the rest of the enclosing run
# ── HONEST LIMIT — `ignore` and `consider` carry no argument ──────── # In UML both operators take a SET OF MESSAGE NAMES — `ignore {t, u}` — # and that set is what makes the claim checkable. `fragment` has no # argument slot, so the names live in the fragment's label, where they # are prose: a reading agent can quote them and attribute them to the # figure, and cannot parse them. The same is true of `loop`'s bounds, # which UML writes `loop(1,3)` and this figure writes into the guard. # # ── HONEST LIMIT — one operator per frame, and no combination ─────── # UML lets an operand of one fragment hold another fragment, and this # genre allows exactly ONE level of that. Twelve sibling frames is what # a demonstrator of the ENUM should be; a figure that also nested them # would be demonstrating the nesting. `dhcp-lease.fd` is where the # nesting is shown, twice.
# ── Semantic classes ─────────────────────────────────────────────── # Three roles, so a reading agent can group the messages by what they # do rather than by which frame they sit in. class session "Opens, uses or closes the session itself" stroke=#2563eb class audit "Written to the audit log — never part of the reply the client sees" stroke=#16a34a class bad "A trace this figure marks as forbidden or as a failure" stroke=#dc2626 style=dashed
lifeline c "Client" lifeline s "Service" lifeline a "Audit log"
# ── loop ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The operand repeats. UML puts the bound in the operator itself, # `loop(1,3)`; here it is in the guard, which is the operand's own # quoted string. fragment open "opening the session" type=loop operand tries "while no response, and fewer than 3 attempts made" in=open message c -> s "POST /session (credentials)" in=tries class=session
# ── alt ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # At most ONE operand runs, and the guards say which. Two operands is # the minimum that makes the operator mean anything. fragment auth "are the credentials accepted?" type=alt operand accepted "accepted" in=auth message c <- s "201 Created (session token)" in=accepted class=session state c "AUTHORIZED" in=accepted operand rejected "rejected" in=auth message c <- s "401 Unauthorized" in=rejected class=bad
# ── assert ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The operand's traces are the ONLY valid continuation at this point: # every trace that reaches here and does something else is invalid. # This is the operator that says MUST, and it is why `type=` has no # default — a frame drawn with no operator would look like this one. fragment mandatory "once a token is issued this MUST follow — nothing else is a valid continuation" type=assert message s -> a "session opened (subject, token id, time)" in=mandatory class=audit
# ── neg ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The operand's traces are INVALID: the figure draws the message in # order to say it must never occur. Drawing a forbidden trace is the # only way to name it, and the frame is what stops it being read as # part of the protocol. fragment forbidden "INVALID traces — the token must never travel in a query string" type=neg message c -> s "GET /profile?token=… (no TLS)" in=forbidden class=bad
# ── critical ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The operand's occurrences may not be interleaved with anything else # on the lifelines it covers — a critical region, not a claim about # duration. fragment atomic "critical region — no other occurrence may interleave on these lifelines" type=critical message s -> a "write: token issued" in=atomic class=audit
# ── par ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The operands interleave in any order, which is the ONE escape from # this genre's total order: two messages that are merely adjacent are # ORDERED, and only a `par` frame says they are not. fragment concurrent "the profile fetch and the audit flush have no relative order" type=par operand fetch "profile fetch" in=concurrent message c -> s "GET /profile" in=fetch class=session operand flush "audit flush" in=concurrent message s -> a "flush buffered records" in=flush class=audit
# ── strict ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The operands are TOTALLY ordered across every lifeline they cover: # nothing in the second may happen before anything in the first, even # on a lifeline the two do not share. fragment twophase "the two steps are totally ordered across BOTH lifelines" type=strict operand prepare "1 — prepare" in=twophase message c -> s "PUT /profile (If-Match: etag)" in=prepare class=session operand commit "2 — commit" in=twophase message c <- s "204 No Content" in=commit class=session
# ── seq ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # Weak sequencing: order is preserved on each lifeline separately and # is unconstrained between lifelines. Here the two operands share the # service, so the service orders them — the client and the audit log # are unordered with respect to each other. fragment weak "weak sequencing — ordered only on the lifeline the two operands share" type=seq operand ask "on the client side" in=weak message c -> s "GET /settings" in=ask class=session operand log "on the audit side" in=weak message s -> a "read: settings" in=log class=audit
# ── opt ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # One operand, run or not run — `alt` with a single operand and no # alternative to choose between. fragment expanded "only when the client asked for the expanded form" type=opt message c <- s "200 OK (expanded profile)" in=expanded class=session
# ── break ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The operand runs INSTEAD OF the rest of the enclosing run: everything # below this frame is abandoned when it fires. That is what makes it # different from `opt`, which returns to the flow it interrupted. fragment giveup "on 503 the remainder of the session is abandoned" type=break message c <- s "503 Service Unavailable" in=giveup class=bad state c "ABANDONED" in=giveup
# ── ignore ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The named messages MAY occur anywhere in this region and are not # significant — so a trace that contains them and a trace that does not # are the same trace as far as this figure is concerned. `<->` is ONE # occurrence: an exchange in both directions whose individual messages # are not enumerated, which is exactly what a heartbeat is. fragment insignificant "ignore {heartbeat} — heartbeats may occur here and mean nothing to this figure" type=ignore message c <-> s "heartbeat" in=insignificant
# ── consider ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # The mirror of `ignore`: ONLY the named messages are significant here, # and anything else that occurs is not. The two are not redundant — # `ignore` names what to drop, `consider` names what to keep, and which # one is shorter to write depends on the region. fragment onlythese "consider {DELETE /session, 204} — nothing else in this region is significant" type=consider message c -> s "DELETE /session" in=onlythese class=session message c <- s "204 No Content" in=onlythese class=session state c "CLOSED"
